wine.name: Dry Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, blended from the house's own vineyards on Seneca Lake and Keuka Lake, with a little bought fruit in some years.
wine.sites: The estate's slopes above the west shore of Keuka Lake, on shale and slate, with blocks planted from 1958 onwards, and its vineyard on Seneca Lake, planted from 2007, which adds riper fruit to the blend.
wine.making: Pressed and fermented cool in temperature controlled stainless steel tanks, kept from malolactic conversion so that the acidity stays sharp, and never put in oak. By the house's sheets the wine then rests on its lees for some months before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Lime, grapefruit and apricot over wet shale, with a hint of petrol in some years that grows with age; light in body and dry to the taste, with high, mouthwatering acidity and a clean, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready on release, it keeps well and gains notes of petrol and honey over five to ten years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with lake trout, sushi or a light chicken dish.

records.table: Grafted vinifera that could live through Finger Lakes winters was the founder's argument, and Dr. Konstantin Frank's Dry Riesling carries it: estate Riesling from Keuka and Seneca Lakes, fermented cool in steel and never oaked, with lime, green apple and wet slate on sharp acidity.
records.story: Konstantin Frank (1899 to 1985), a viticulturist from Odessa who had grown Riesling in the hard winters of Ukraine, reached New York in 1951 with a doctorate in viticulture and, by the house's account, little English. He worked at the Geneva Experiment Station, where he argued against the received view that European vines could not live through the region's cold. In 1953 he met the head of Gold Seal, a French champagne maker who shared his French and who, by the house's account, hired him that year; together they made experimental plantings that showed grafted vinifera on the right rootstock could come through the winter. In 1958 Frank bought land on the west side of Keuka Lake and planted Riesling and other European varieties, and in 1962 he founded Vinifera Wine Cellars, a name that declared its purpose. His son, who had bought a separate property in the early 1980s for traditional method sparkling wine, ran the house after his death in 1985, and the family has kept it since, across four generations by its own account. The Dry Riesling puts the founder's case into a bottle: a vinifera wine of the Finger Lakes that needs no hybrid grape and no excuse, and with it the region's Riesling story opens.

The Dry Riesling blends estate fruit from two lakes, so it carries the wider Finger Lakes name rather than a single lake's appellation.

wine.name: HJW Vineyard Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from the estate's own vines in the HJW Vineyard.
wine.sites: The HJW Vineyard, the founder's home site above the west shore of Seneca Lake near Dundee, planted from 1976 to 1978 on shallow topsoil over shale bedrock that keeps yields low; farmed biodynamically, with Demeter certification from 2023.
wine.making: Picked and sorted by hand, pressed as whole clusters and fermented slowly with the vineyard's own yeasts in stainless steel, where it stays for some months before bottling. It is made dry or close to it, with less than a per cent of sugar left in the vintages read.
wine.glass: Lime zest, tangerine peel and green apple over crushed stone and white pepper, with white peach and a hint of white blossom in some years; taut and lean in body, with high, piercing acidity and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after three to five and gains depth for a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a white wine glass, with trout, scallops or roast pork.

records.table: Above Seneca Lake, on shale the founder planted in the late 1970s, grows the HJW Vineyard Riesling of Hermann J. Wiemer Vineyard: hand picked, fermented with its own yeasts in steel and dry or nearly so. Lime, tangerine peel and stone ride taut acidity; pour it cool.
records.story: Bernkastel on the Mosel was the founder's home, in a family that had made wine there for generations, and he trained at Geisenheim. In 1968 he chose the Finger Lakes over the family business and went to work as winemaker at Bully Hill, near Hammondsport on Keuka Lake, where he also began grafting vinifera vines. In 1973 he bought a former soybean farm above the west shore of Seneca Lake near Dundee, where no commercial Riesling then grew, and from 1976 to 1978 he planted Riesling and Chardonnay there, the block that became the HJW Vineyard. By the house's account his first wines, a Riesling and a Chardonnay, came out in 1979, the year it gives for the founding, though one trade account puts his first wines for sale in 1981, after he left Bully Hill. Beside the cellar he built a grafting nursery that supplied vines to growers across the East. In 2007 he retired and handed the estate to his winemaker, with a Swedish agronomist as partner, and the single vineyard bottlings grew under them. In 2023 the HJW Vineyard gained Demeter certification for biodynamic farming. What one Finger Lakes site on shale gives Riesling is the HJW Vineyard's lesson: the Mosel's teaching, written in another country's stone.

records.table: Gravel over limestone, on a steep slope of the early 1980s above Seneca Lake's southeast shore, gives Ravines Wine Cellars its Argetsinger Vineyard Dry Riesling, fermented cool in steel and kept on its lees. Key lime, grapefruit and wet stone, dry and taut; try it with trout.
records.story: Ravines was founded by a couple, a European trained winemaker raised on his family's Provence estate and a chef, who set out to make truly dry Riesling in a region where few made one. In 1998 the winemaker became head winemaker at Dr. Konstantin Frank, where by the house's account he stayed until 2005. In 2000 the couple bought a parcel on the steep eastern slopes of Keuka Lake between two deep ravines, which carry cold air and water away from the vines and gave the house its name, and by its own account the house was founded in 2001. Its first vintage, of 2002, was all dry vinifera wine, and its Dry Riesling soon took the prize for dry Riesling at the World Riesling Cup, as the house tells it. From the start the house drew Riesling from the Argetsinger Vineyard on Seneca Lake, owned and farmed by the Argetsinger family. Vineyards on each side of Seneca Lake, among them 16 Falls and White Springs, followed from 2003 and 2004. The winemaking later moved to Geneva, at the north end of Seneca Lake. One Seneca site on limestone, made dry: the Argetsinger wine measures how far Finger Lakes Riesling has travelled from sweetness.

records.table: One clone, Geisenheim 239, chosen for its sharper acidity, makes Boundary Breaks' No. 239 Dry Riesling, grown at Lodi near Seneca Lake's east shore. Lime, green apple and flint, dry and bright, let a guest taste what a clone alone gives.
records.story: The land on Porter Covert Road at Lodi, on the east side of Seneca Lake, was bought by the Covert family in 1861 and stayed in the family as farmland for more than a century; after the last of them died in 1967 it was rented to other farmers. In 2008 most of the farm was sold to the estate's founder, who found on it only a half built cabin, and by the house's account the estate dates from that year. From 2009 the vineyard was planted almost wholly to Riesling. Rather than one clone, the estate planted several, among them Geisenheim clones 198 and 239, to see how each would show on the site, and it chose to bottle them apart: 239, slightly sharper in acidity, for a dry wine, and 198 for a reserve. The young vines gave the estate's first wines, released in 2013 by its own account. The estate is young and its story short, but it has a clear idea, the clone on the label as other houses print a vineyard, and the No. 239 Dry Riesling carries it. A clone, and not only a site, can mark a Riesling, and the Finger Lakes have room for both.

wine.name: Classique Dry Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, blended from growers' vineyards along the east shore of Seneca Lake.
wine.sites: Ten to sixteen lieux dits, by vintage, along an eight mile stretch of the east shore of Seneca Lake, among them sites the house also bottles alone, such as Caywood, Railroad and Willow.
wine.making: Each site is pressed and fermented apart, spontaneously, with its own yeasts in neutral barrels in the vintages read, with some steel in earlier years, and the lots are then blended. The wine is made bone dry, with almost no sugar left.
wine.glass: Mirabelle plum, bergamot and lemon zest over chamomile and wet stone, with apple skin in some years; bone dry and taut, light to medium in body, with bright acidity and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, it gains texture over three to six years and keeps longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with shellfish, roast pork or a light curry.

records.table: Many growers' sites along Seneca Lake's east shore go into Forge Cellars' Dry Riesling Classique, each fermented apart with its own yeasts, much of it in old barrels, as a Rhône grower would work. Bone dry, with plum, bergamot and wet stone; serve it cool beside shellfish.
records.story: Forge Cellars began in 2011, eight years after Seneca Lake became an appellation of its own in 2003, as a partnership between a grower and winemaker of the southern Rhône, of the family that holds Château de Saint Cosme in Gigondas, and American partners, one of whom found the fruit and oversaw the growing. The aim, by the house's account, was bone dry Riesling from Seneca Lake to stand beside the dry Rieslings of Alsace and Germany. The first vintage, of 2011, was a small lot of dry Riesling, and over the following years the house grew to many bottlings, Riesling and Pinot Noir above all, from growers' sites along the east shore. The blend of those sites carries the name Classique, while the sites that stood out are bottled alone under their own names, such as Railroad, crossed by the old ties of the Lehigh Valley Railroad. The winery is at Burdett, on the southeast shore. The method is the Rhône partner's: each site pressed and fermented apart with its own yeasts in neutral barrels, then blended. Forge Cellars is a house of its own, not a branch of Saint Cosme. The Classique gathers Seneca Lake's east shore into one wine, read through a European cellar: the bottle to learn before the site wines.

traps: Forge Cellars is a Seneca Lake house of its own, founded with a partner from Château de Saint Cosme; it is neither a Gigondas wine nor a label of Saint Cosme.
Classique is the blend of many sites; the single vineyard Rieslings, such as Caywood or Railroad, carry their site's name instead.

cards.front: Forge Cellars: what does Classique on the label mean?
cards.back: The house's blend of many sites along Seneca Lake's east shore, each fermented apart before blending.

cards.front: From which Rhône house's family came the founding partner of Forge Cellars?
cards.back: Château de Saint Cosme in Gigondas; the partnership with American partners began in 2011.

questions.q: A guest asks how Forge Cellars ferments its Dry Riesling Classique. Which answer fits?
opts: Site by site, own yeasts, neutral barrels
All together in steel, selected yeasts
In new oak with full malolactic
In concrete eggs, then on the skins
questions.exp: Each site is fermented apart with its own yeasts, much of it in neutral barrels, and then blended; one blend fermented in steel with selected yeasts is not the Forge way.

questions.q: In what year did Forge Cellars make its first dry Riesling from Seneca Lake?
questions.exp: The partnership began with the 2011 vintage; 1979 is the year of Hermann J. Wiemer's opening vintage and 2002 that of Ravines.

report: The house's own pages print the label Dry Riesling Classique; the record keeps the plan's order, Classique Dry Riesling, which the lint requires, and the integrator may wish to reorder the plan's wine to the label's form (a rename, not a swap).
The number of sites in the blend varies by vintage (ten in 2023, sixteen in 2021, by the house's pages), so the record says ten to sixteen, by vintage.
The Seneca Lake appellation follows the house's listings and Wine Spectator; one retailer gives the 2017 as the first so labelled, a single source, so the record gives no year for it.
Living names met and never written: the three partners, the Rhône partner among them; they may belong in people.json.
Refuter: 'Classique since the 2014 vintage' is refuted by a Classique Dry Riesling 2013 listed by a merchant, and cut; the first vintage of 2011 rests on the importer's and a merchant's accounts.

changed: wine.making, label, card and story: 'Classique since the 2014 vintage' is refuted by a Classique Dry Riesling 2013 listed by a merchant, and cut everywhere.

wine.making: fermentation in neutral barrels is now 'in the vintages read', with some steel in earlier years, since the 2021 and 2023 pages give neutral barrel and a 2017 listing a share in steel; the table follows.

story: 'sits high above Burdett' cut to 'is at Burdett', the address on the house's sheet; the Railroad site and the Lehigh Valley ties added from Decanter; the Seneca Lake appellation of 2003 added as a dated turning point from TTB.
wine.glass: was plum, lemon oil, grapefruit and salt; now Mirabelle plum, bergamot, lemon zest, chamomile and apple skin from reviews of 2013, 2015 and 2023 quoted by the house.
questions: the wine explanation no longer pins selected yeasts on Dr. Konstantin Frank, which no sheet read confirmed.
open: The number of sites in the blend is 13 in Decanter against ten and sixteen on the house's pages; the record's ten to sixteen, by vintage, stands on the house.
